summary: TRILL uses distribution trees to deliver multi-destination frames, and multiple trees may be used by an ingress RBridge. This proposed standard describes how data labels, such as VLAN or Fine-Grained Label, can be used to choose among those trees so different traffic can be spread across them.

plainLanguage.summary: When many people need to get the same announcement, several delivery routes can share the work. This lets the network pick which route to use based on a label on the traffic.

subtitle: Letting TRILL assign each VLAN or label to particular distribution trees so forwarding tables stay small.

tldr.problem: When an RBridge may send any VLAN or label on any of several distribution trees, its multicast forwarding table grows by the number of trees, and fast-path hardware has limited room.
tldr.mechanism: The highest-priority tree root announces which VLANs, FGLs or multicast groups are allowed on each tree, and ingress RBridges announce which of those trees they will actually use, via six new APPsub-TLVs.
tldr.outcome: If each VLAN is allowed on only one tree, table size drops by the number of trees, while load is still balanced. Older RBridges keep working, but the saving is smaller in a mixed campus.

sections.title: Distribution Trees in a TRILL Campus
sections.content:
In a TRILL campus (a network of TRILL switches, also called RBridges), multi-destination frames travel along distribution trees identified by their root nicknames. The RBridge with the highest tree root priority announces how many trees to compute, and each RBridge says which trees it will use for traffic it originates, using the TREE-USE-IDs sub-TLV from RFC 7176.

To avoid wasting link capacity, trees are pruned per VLAN or Fine-Grained Label (FGL), cutting branches with no downstream receivers, as RFC 6325 specifies. Pruning on Layer 2 or Layer 3 multicast addresses is also possible. How many trees exist, where the roots sit and which trees an ingress uses are left to the implementation.

The data center case brings a twist. In a typical fat tree, the tree roots sit on aggregation switches (RB1 and RB2 in the RFC's figure), so every ingress access switch is equally distant from all roots.
sections.plainLanguage: A distribution tree is a delivery route that reaches everyone who needs a copy. Pruning means not sending trucks down streets where nobody wants the delivery.

sections.title: The Forwarding Table Problem
sections.content:
With equal-cost closest roots, an ingress RBridge can use one tree only, which makes link usage uneven, or spread traffic among trees with an ECMP-like method. The second option makes the multicast forwarding table grow linearly with the number of trees.

Such a table maps a key of tree nickname plus VLAN to a list of ports. With n trees and m VLANs, the table has n*m entries. Using FGLs or finer pruning increases m, and more trees for load balancing increase n. The RFC's example: four trees and 4K VLANs with downstream receivers take 16K entries. Fast-path hardware tables are limited, and some share space with Layer 3 IP multicast for a total of 16K or 8K entries.

Not pruning is not a general fix. It wastes bandwidth on broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast such as IPTV, it does not help edge nodes that must decide how to replicate frames to access ports, and it weakens VLAN or FGL isolation and so risks leakage of traffic.

The RFC also notes that some silicon does not support hash-based tree selection at the ingress but commonly selects the tree by VLAN. This document is compatible with that.
sections.plainLanguage: If every street could use every truck, each post office needs a note for every street and truck pair. That pile of notes gets too big for the small filing cabinet in the machine.

sections.title: Tree Selection Based on Data Labels
sections.content:
A Data Label is a VLAN or an FGL. The RBridge with the highest priority to be a tree root announces the tree nicknames and the Data Labels allowed on each tree, from static configuration or a predefined algorithm outside the scope of the document. An ingress RBridge picks from that list and SHOULD NOT send VLAN x frames on tree y unless the announcement allows it.

If each VLAN is allowed on only one tree, the table can be held at 4K entries at most, or up to 16M for FGLs. The RFC's example appoints tree 1 to carry VLANs 1-2000 and tree 2 to carry VLANs 2001-4094, so no RBridge stores tree 1 with VLAN 2001-4094 or tree 2 with VLAN 1-2000. The entry count falls by a factor f, the number of trees, from 2*4094 to 4094 in the example. This helps both transit and edge nodes, and the data-plane encoding does not change.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss says street numbers 1 to 2000 use truck 1 and the rest use truck 2. Now nobody needs notes for a street riding the wrong truck.

sections.title: The Six APPsub-TLVs
sections.content:
Six new APPsub-TLVs are carried in the TRILL GENINFO TLV in E-L1FS FS-LSPs. They come in announce and use pairs:

  • Tree and VLANs (type 11) and Tree and VLANs Used (12)
  • Tree and FGLs (13) and Tree and FGLs Used (14)
  • Tree and Groups (15) and Tree and Groups Used (16)

The first of each pair is sent by the highest-priority tree root to say what is allowed. The "Used" form is sent by an ingress RBridge to say what it selected.

The VLAN form holds 6-byte Tree-VLAN records: a 2-byte tree nickname, then Start.VLAN and End.VLAN, each with 4 reserved bits that MUST be sent as zero. The FGL form has 8-byte records: a nickname, then 3-byte Start.FGL and End.FGL. Length is 6*n or 8*n, and a Length that is not a multiple makes the APPsub-TLV corrupt, so it MUST be ignored. A record whose End is less than its Start MUST be ignored. A single value appears as both start and end.

The Groups form carries a tree nickname plus Group sub-sub-TLVs of the kind allowed inside a GADDR TLV, each naming a multicast group and a VLAN or FGL. It lets the root put, for example, group 1 in VLAN 10 on tree 1 and group 2 in VLAN 10 on tree 2.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of lists: by street, by big-city district and by club. For each kind, the boss posts what is allowed, and each sender posts what it picked.

sections.title: Processing Rules and Failure Handling
sections.content:
The highest-priority tree root MUST still include all the usual tree-related sub-TLVs and MAY add the TREE-VLANs and TREE-FGLs APPsub-TLVs. An ingress that understands them SHOULD choose its tree-VLAN pairs and advertise them in TREE-VLAN-USE APPsub-TLVs. If several trees are allowed for a VLAN, how to choose is out of scope, though a fixed algorithm so all ingresses agree may be desirable. Ideally each Data Label maps to one tree, but any mapping to fewer than all trees helps.

When encapsulating a frame for Data Label x, an ingress SHOULD use the tree it advertised. If it advertised none, it can use any tree the root allows for that label. A pruning RBridge uses the USE APPsub-TLVs to mark which VLANs or FGLs are reachable downstream per adjacency and tree. An ingress that does not support the feature is logically like one that announces all trees for all VLANs and FGLs.

On failure, if a non-highest-priority root fails, the highest-priority root should reassign its VLANs to other trees or a replacement. If the highest-priority root fails, the RFC suggests pre-configuring the second-highest root with the proper tree-VLAN correspondence, matching the highest root for the other trees, to minimize table changes. Larger campuses may do the same on lower roots.

If no tree is allowed for VLAN x, or its tree root is unreachable and no alternative exists, the ingress should be downgraded to a conventional RBridge per RFC 6325. A timer should delay this, set to at least the LSP flooding time of the campus.
sections.plainLanguage: If the truck boss quits, the second-in-charge already has the same plan on file, so nobody has to rewrite their notes. If no truck is available, you fall back to the old way.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
RBridges MUST keep including the TREE-USE-IDs and INT-VLAN sub-TLVs when RFC 6325 requires, whether or not they support the new APPsub-TLVs. A receiver that understands TREE-VLAN-USE from a given RBridge uses it for the multicast table and ignores that RBridge's TREE-USE-IDs and INT-VLAN for that purpose. They remain useful for other things, such as building an RPF table and spanning tree root notification. If no TREE-VLAN-USE arrives, the conventional method applies.

The RFC's example has RB2 (new) interested in VLANs 10 and 11, using tree 1 for VLAN 10 and tree 2 for VLAN 11, and RB3 (old) interested in VLANs 100 and 101. RB1 builds two entries for RB2 but four for RB3, one per tree and VLAN. The merged table is therefore bigger than if every RBridge supported the feature.

In the worst case of a hybrid campus the table is as large as today's practice. That happens when the new RBridges' interested VLANs are a subset of the old ones'. Effectiveness grows as more RBridges support the feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Old post offices don't read the new notes, so they still need notes for every truck. Only the new ones save space, so the more that switch, the better.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The document does not change the general RBridge security considerations of the TRILL base protocol, which RFC 6325 covers in its Section 6. The new APPsub-TLVs can be secured with IS-IS authentication from RFC 5310.

IANA assigned six APPsub-TLV types, 11 through 16, in the "TRILL APPsub-TLV Types under IS-IS TLV 251 Application Identifier 1" registry.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds no new risks beyond the ones TRILL already has, and the new messages can be signed like other routing messages.
